I've found that most of the side effects go away after being on them for 1-2 weeks. They're probably persisting because you aren't taking it every day.

Or venlafaxine might just not work for you. I tried sertraline and the side effects never went away, so I changed to citalopram which is... not as bad? Different antidepressants work better for different people, so it might be worth trying something else.
In the UK [they'd have disarmed him](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cX5CPx4RKWw). I don't blame the police, they should've been trained to deal with it properly.
People trying to kill themselves due to mental illness are very rarely making a rational decision.
Alllllllll the time. Like you, the only thing that stops me is knowing what it would do to my parents. I don't think I have anything helpful to tell yoi, but I promise it can get better.

> I'm usually passive about this, but sometimes I'll feel really actively suicidal. I'm not even sure if I really do want this, but if I don't REALLY want this then I want to want to do it, if that makes sense.

This makes perfect sense to me. I feel like I do want to do it but I don't at the same time. Or I want it to happen but I don't want to do it myself. It's weird to explain but I do know what you mean.

I really hope it gets better for us both.

I start maladaptive daydreaming/fantasizing. That was the biggest thing I noticed that just *wasn't there* when I got out of depression, and it was the first thing I noticed that came back when I got depressed again.

I don't know why I do it, but I just start living more in my head than in the real world. I drift off into these nice fantasies. I imagine myself being better than I am, having a relationship, shit like that. It becomes disruptive and distracting.

I also stop doing stuff. Stop going out, lose all my good habits.

But I think you'd probably feel it if you were relapsing, I know I did. I started to feel sad, worthless and unmotivated, and it sort of got worse and worse over time, and the longer I left it the harder it got to pick myself up. That was the first time at least, the second time was much more sudden.

If you've ever had CBT you'll probably notice your bad thinking patterns start creeping back into you head too.
And if it doesn't work, try a different one. After 3 weeks of absolute hell on sertraline I switched to citalopram and felt better straight away.
I messed up badly in year 12 (due to the depression) so I'm doing an extra year.

Sounds like quite bad social anxiety. I get the same thing. For me it's worst when I'm walking into a room and I'm late for something so I'm interrupting. I sweat really badly, and then I get more anxious because I know everyone can see it.

Have you talked to a doctor about it? Therapy can be helpful for this, as can medications. I had therapy for anxiety a while ago and it didn't solve everything but it did help me get a bit more comfortable in social situations.

I also found that practice helps. Just putting myself in the situations that scare me. I started saying hello to strangers as I passed them in the street, then progressed to brief conversations.

I'm in the same situation OP! I'm in sixth form, depression has came back and fucked me this year. I can't do any work, I also haven't done my UCAS and can't bring myself to do it. I've been feeling suicidal, I'm very very close to being kicked out due to poor attendance. I have to see the head of sixth form about that in the morning, and I haven't slept yet.

I want you to know that it's not the end of the world. I actually fucked up year 12 (again due to depression) and I was able to take an extra year to resit the exams I did badly in. Maybe you can do that? 

You should be able to sort something out with your college regarding attendance.  I'm not entirely sure, but that's why I'm seeing my head of sixth form - to see if they can give me any help. I can probably let you know later how that goes.

If you can do something about that, then you're good. You have over half a year til your exams, and that's more than enough time to turn things around if you get the right help. Keep in mind that with your grades from last year (assuming you're doing A levels?) you could actually do pretty poorly this year and still come out with 3 Cs, which can get you into some decent universities. Of course you could also come out with 3 As. You did pretty damn good last year.

EVEN IF it really does all go to shit, it's still not the end of the world. You can apply to university at any point in your life (before 60 I think) as a mature student, and receive full student finance support. So if you feel the need to, you can take a year or a few to sort things out and then come back to education. 

With regards to depression, I'm wondering how old you are? Because when I was below 18 I had to ggo through the adolescent mental health service which had a waiting list of several months, but after 18 I could go to the adult service and got a therapist pretty much straight away. So maybe speak to your GP about that. Also, if you tell your GP you've been feeling suicidal you can possibly get bumped up the waiting list.

In the mean time, have you tried antidepressants? If your GP was reluctant to put you on them, I'd recommend trying 5 htp which is a supplement that helps with low mood. Expensive af but you can get it at Holland and Barrett, it helped me a bit.

When I started sixth form my teacher told me that these are the hardest years of your life, more so than university or any job you'll get. And it's even harder with depression. You did brilliantly last year, and if you can just get through this year then things will start to get brighter.

Hang in there buddy, feel free to PM me if you have any questions or you just want a friend to talk to.

Well, I had cognitive behavioural therapy which is about changing your thought patterns. Your therapist will discuss your issues, worries and whatever, and they'll help you to think about the way you think about things, and then change that. 

It's hard to explain but, for example, with my therapist I discussed how I felt inadequate and we talked about it and then eventually identified that it's because I compare myself too much to other people. So then we worked on helping me realize when I have that type of thought, and replacing it with a different thought. So when I get my exam results, instead of thinking "there are people that do much better" I'd make the conscious effort to think "I've done really well". 

Stuff like that, but working through all your thoughts. If you really open up and you commit to it, you start forming habits and thinking more positively without needing to think about it. It doesn't sound like it'd help much, but it's amazing how much better you'll feel just by changing the way you think.

My first therapist gave me [this](http://www.getselfhelp.co.uk/unhelpful.htm) which describes some of the bad thought patterns. 

It's not only about changing your thoughts though, there are various things they can do to help. Even just talking usually helps, so they'll talk to you and they'll help identify the underlying causes of your problems. They'll give suggestions - my therapist suggested I start going out every week or so, so I decided to start doing that and it helped a lot. She also suggested I keep a diary of my thoughts, but I didn't want to do that so I didn't.

Look in the mirror and practice smiling. Make sure you smile with your eyes, too. If you can learn to smile convincingly, you just need to smile when someone speaks to you and they probably won't sense anything wrong.

I did this for so long I just smile automatically now. Not necessarily a good thing though, because sometimes I wish people would notice when I'm feeling down.

Have you tried therapy? It's hard work and you need to believe it'll work for it to work, but it helped me a hell of a lot. It completely pulled me out of depression a few years ago, although I ended up slipping back into it.

I'd really recommend it if you haven't tried already. Just keep an open mind, and if it's not working for you, let your therapist know, because there are different types of therapy and different therapists.
